clue.text: Row about double parking of truck

indicators.note: about means the first piece goes round the second, holding it in the middle

parts.note: a row of seats is a tier

indicators.note: double here asks for the parking abbreviation to be written out twice in a row

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for parking on road signs

explanation.surface: A complaint about a lorry blocking traffic by parking in the second lane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Double parking' looks like a motoring offence but just means P twice, set inside TIER.
explanation.definitionFit: A tipper is a lorry whose load bed tilts to dump its contents, so it is a kind of truck.

clue.text: As a rule, the responsibility of quartermasters?

definitions.text: As a rule, the responsibility of quartermasters?

parts.words: As a rule, the responsibility of quartermasters?
parts.note: quartermasters is read as masters of quarters, four rulers each holding a quarter, and rule is government

explanation.surface: Claiming that something is normally the job of army supply officers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As a rule' means usually on the surface but here refers to government; quartermasters become four joint rulers.
explanation.definitionFit: A tetrarchy is government by four people, each ruling a quarter, so it is a rule shared by four masters.

clue.text: Reading of The Country Girl

parts.note: Peru is a country in South America
Sal is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A performance or reading of a play called The Country Girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reading' looks like a stage reading of a play but means close study; 'of The' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A perusal is a careful reading through, as of a document.

clue.text: Without it en suite, what's to come next?

indicators.note: without here means lacking, so the following letters are taken out

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Wondering what happens next in a hotel room with no private bathroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'en suite' is a bathroom attached to a bedroom; taking IT out leaves the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to follow afterwards as a result, which is to come next.

clue.text: Means of examining approaches to the labyrinth

definitions.text: Means of examining approaches to the labyrinth

parts.words: Means of examining approaches to the labyrinth
parts.note: the labyrinth is the anatomical name for the inner ear, so this describes a medical instrument for looking down the ear canal that leads to it

explanation.surface: Someone surveying the paths leading into a maze.
explanation.walkthrough: The labyrinth here is not a maze but the inner ear; its approach is the outer ear canal, which a doctor inspects with a lighted instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: An otoscope is the lighted viewer a doctor uses to look into the ear canal, which leads toward the inner ear's labyrinth.

clue.text: Interest the law, possibly, in dramatic affairs of Sicilians

indicators.note: possibly signals that these letters could form another arrangement

explanation.surface: The Mafia take an interest in the law in their theatrical business.
explanation.walkthrough: The Shakespeare play opens at the court of Sicily, so its drama is literally the affairs of Sicilians.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's late play is set partly at the Sicilian court of King Leontes, so it dramatises events among Sicilians.

clue.text: Entrapped spirit that gets rattled when beaten

parts.note: to be entrapped is to be snared
rum is a spirit made from sugar cane

explanation.surface: A trapped drinker who becomes flustered when defeated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rattled' and 'beaten' suggest a flustered loser, but describe a drum whose wires rattle when struck.
explanation.definitionFit: This drum has wires stretched across its lower skin that buzz against it when the top is struck.

clue.text: Tangle that might interfere with boat's propeller?

definitions.meaning: tangle is the name of a large brown seaweed, a kelp

definitions.text: that might interfere with boat's propeller?
definitions.meaning: a weed fouling a rowing boat's oar, the thing that propels it

explanation.surface: A knot of something fouling the screw of a motorboat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tangle' is not a knot but a kelp seaweed; the second part jokes about weed snagging an oar.
explanation.definitionFit: Tangle is a common name for a kelp seaweed, the same plant also known by this name.

clue.text: Antelope seen in English countryside

parts.note: land can mean rural country, as in working the land

explanation.surface: An African antelope spotted in the English countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen in' only links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The eland is a large African antelope with spiralled horns.

clue.text: Walk like some monarchs

definitions.meaning: a stroll taken for the sake of one's health
describing a king or queen whose powers are limited by law

explanation.surface: Strolling in a regal manner.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a health-giving stroll, and a monarch bound by a constitution is called this.

clue.text: Flier sets course for Newcastle?

annotationWithheld.why: Flier sets course for Newcastle? (9): the bird TURNSTONE is clear, but no parse accounts for 'sets course for Newcastle' with confidence (possibly turns at Stone, a Staffordshire town near Newcastle-under-Lyme), and no blog was found to confirm it

clue.text: Vessel carrying vital stuff from China or Taiwan

indicators.note: from tells us the letters are taken out of the run of words China or Taiwan that follows

explanation.surface: A ship transporting essential cargo out of East Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'chinA OR TAiwan'. 'Vessel' suggests a ship, but it is a blood vessel carrying blood.
explanation.definitionFit: The aorta is the body's main artery, the blood vessel taking oxygenated blood from the heart.

clue.text: Man, for example, added to a division in church

parts.note: the Isle of Man is an example of an island, so Man stands for isle

explanation.surface: A man joining one of the factions in a church dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man, an island in the Irish Sea, not a person; 'added to' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An aisle is a side section of a church nave, separated off by pillars, so it is a division of the building.

clue.text: He takes care of litter wind here's disturbed

indicators.note: disturbed means the letters of wind here's are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A pig-keeper bothered by rubbish blowing about in the wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter' is a brood of piglets, not rubbish; the letters of WIND HERES are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A swineherd looks after pigs, and a litter is a set of young born to a sow.

clue.text: Person committing slander left a main court, free

indicators.note: free here means loose, so the letters are released into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone guilty of slander walking out of the principal court without penalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'free' looks like the verdict but is the anagram signal for L plus A MAIN COURT.
explanation.definitionFit: A calumniator spreads calumny, false and damaging statements about someone, which is slander.

clue.text: Bungle organisation of main games

indicators.note: organisation of means the letters of main games are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: Botching the running of the principal sporting events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organisation of' looks like admin but signals that MAIN GAMES is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To mismanage something is to handle it badly, which is to bungle it.

clue.text: Money received by auditor as note

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so what the listener receives is how the word sounds when spoken

parts.note: dough is slang for money

explanation.surface: Cash taken in by a financial auditor, recorded as a banknote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' looks like an accountant but means a listener; DOUGH sounds like DOH, the first note of the sol-fa scale.
explanation.definitionFit: Doh is the first degree of the tonic sol-fa scale, so it is a musical note.

clue.text: Ready to keep quiet

parts.note: ready is slang for cash, as in the readies, so this is cash paid to buy someone's silence

explanation.surface: Someone prepared to stay silent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is not willing but cash (the readies), the bribe paid for silence.
explanation.definitionFit: Hush money is a payment made to stop someone revealing a secret.

clue.text: Tropical climber seen in English tree? Just the opposite

indicators.note: just the opposite tells us to turn the word around and read it in the other direction

parts.note: may is the English name for the hawthorn tree

explanation.surface: A tropical vine found growing in an English tree, or rather the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: MAY, the hawthorn, written backwards. 'Seen in' only links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The yam is a tropical vine grown for its starchy tubers, a twining climbing plant.

clue.text: Turning effects of mechanics, in seconds

definitions.meaning: in physics, the turning effect of a force about a point is its torque, measured as force times distance
seconds as in short intervals of time, as in just a sec

explanation.surface: Engineers measuring rotation within a few seconds.
explanation.definitionFit: In physics the term names a force's turning effect, and in speech it means brief instants of time.

clue.text: Settle new males into satisfactory courses

parts.note: to settle a debt is to square it

indicators.note: new means the letters of males are made into something fresh

explanation.surface: Introducing new men into worthwhile training programmes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courses' are parts of a meal, not training; MALES rearranged gives MEALS.
explanation.definitionFit: A square meal is a full, nourishing one, so these are satisfying dinners rather than classes.

clue.text: Status of a Rugby Union team turning out? Not necessarily nowadays

definitions.text: Status of a Rugby Union team turning out? Not necessarily nowadays

indicators.note: turning out signals that the preceding letters are turned into another order

explanation.surface: Asking whether a rugby side playing unpaid is still the norm since the game went professional.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby Union allowed professionals in 1995, hence 'not necessarily nowadays'. 'turning out' looks like fielding a side but rearranges A, RU and TEAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugby Union players were long required to be unpaid, a status the sport dropped in 1995.

clue.text: Striking player in North is welcomed by one boy after another

indicators.note: after puts the second boy's piece following the first

parts.note: Tim is a boy's name

indicators.note: being welcomed by someone means being taken in, so the first piece holds the next inside

parts.note: Pat is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A footballer on strike in the North, greeted by one lad after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' suggests industrial action but describes a percussionist who hits drums; 'in' is only a link word, and 'one boy after another' means two different boys' names.
explanation.definitionFit: A timpanist plays the kettledrums, hitting them with sticks, so he is a player who strikes his instrument.

clue.text: Carry to mass a symbolic image

parts.note: to tote is to carry
M is the abbreviation for mass in physics

explanation.surface: Bringing a sacred picture along to church services.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mass' suggests a church service but is the physics abbreviation M; 'to' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem is an emblem, often carved, standing for a clan or tribe.

clue.text: Army quarters taking detachment

parts.note: south and west are two quarters of the compass, abbreviated S and W
an arm is a branch or division of a larger force

explanation.surface: Soldiers' barracks receiving a unit of troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Army' is a crowd, not soldiers; 'taking' simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Army can mean a vast crowd, as in an army of ants, which is a swarm.

clue.text: It makes a good deal of sense

definitions.text: It makes a good deal of sense

parts.words: It makes a good deal of sense
parts.note: one of the five senses, and also a colloquial word for a lot, as in a far better

explanation.surface: Praising something as very reasonable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes sense' suggests reasonableness; the answer is one of the senses and also slang for a great deal.
explanation.definitionFit: Vision is one of the five senses, and in casual speech 'a far better' uses this word to mean much.

clue.text: Vehicle used in India and Pacific islands

definitions.meaning: a light horse-drawn two-wheeled carriage of the Indian subcontinent
a Polynesian kingdom made up of islands in the South Pacific

explanation.surface: A form of transport found in both India and the South Seas.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word names an Indian horse-drawn cart and a Polynesian island kingdom.

clue.text: Alternative colour of flower that's normally blue or white

definitions.text: Alternative colour of flower that's normally blue or white

parts.words: Alternative colour of flower that's normally blue or white
parts.note: a flower is something that flows, a river; the river with Blue and White branches is given a third colour

explanation.surface: A garden flower usually blue or white appearing in another shade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is a river (it flows): the Nile has Blue and White branches, so a different colour of it is a pale bluish green.
explanation.definitionFit: Nile green is a pale bluish-green shade, named after the river whose two main branches are called Blue and White.

clue.text: Got off to a bad start at Newmarket?

definitions.text: Got off to a bad start at Newmarket?

parts.words: Got off to a bad start at Newmarket?
parts.note: Newmarket is a card game as well as a racecourse town, and the opening of any card game is handing out the cards, so a bad start is a botched hand-out

explanation.surface: A racehorse breaking badly from the stalls at the Newmarket races.
explanation.walkthrough: Newmarket is a Suffolk town famous for horse racing, but it is also a card game; starting badly there means giving out the cards wrongly.
explanation.definitionFit: To misdeal is to distribute cards incorrectly, the poor beginning of a round of a card game.

clue.text: Part of the week-end when articles are removed for firm

indicators.note: are removed tells us letters are taken out of the weekend day

parts.note: Saturday is one of the two days of the weekend
a is the indefinite article; two of them give two letters A

explanation.surface: Part of the weekend when shop goods are cleared out for a company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company but is the adjective; both As go from SATURDAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Sturdy means strongly built and solid, which is what firm describes.
